questions.q: Minimum number of stories recommended to be provided with at least 3 approved recording accelerographs.
questions.n: Standard building codes specify this height as the minimum for providing a set of three accelerographs.

questions.q: Maintenance and service of accelerographs shall be provided by the ______.
questions.n: The responsibility for the upkeep and operational costs of building safety equipment lies with the property owner.

questions.q: Who shall be responsible for keeping the actual live load below the allowable limits and shall be liable for any failure on the structure due to overloading.
questions.n: The party using the space is legally responsible for ensuring they do not exceed the design weight limits.

questions.q: The period of continuous application of a given load or the aggregate of periods of intermittent application of the same load.
questions.n: This term defines the total time a load acts on a structure, which is critical for material fatigue analysis.

questions.q: Minimum area in square meters a member supports which the design live load may be reduced.
questions.n: National building codes permit live load reduction for members supporting influence areas of at least this size.

questions.q: Minimum height of any wall requiring structural design to resist loads onto which they are subjected.
questions.n: Standard regulations require any wall exceeding this height to be formally analyzed for structural stability.

questions.q: Maximum deflection of a brittle finished wall subjected to a load of 250 Pascal applied perpendicular to said wall.
questions.n: Brittle finishes require stiffer support to prevent cracking, thus a tighter deflection limit is used.

questions.q: Maximum deflection of a flexible finished wall subjected to a load of 250 Pascal applied perpendicular to said wall.
questions.n: Flexible finishes can tolerate more movement, allowing for a higher deflection ratio.

questions.q: Maximum floor area for a low-cost housing unit.
questions.n: Statutory definitions for low-cost housing typically cap the allowable floor area at this value.

questions.q: The level at which the earthquake motions are considered to be imparted to the structure or the level at which the structure, as a dynamic vibrator, is supported.
questions.n: The base is the theoretical plane where the structure is considered to transition into the ground for seismic analysis.

questions.q: A member or an element provided to transfer lateral forces from a portion of a structure to vertical elements of the lateral force resisting system.
questions.n: A collector 'collects' lateral loads from a floor or roof and 'drags' them into the vertical resisting elements.

questions.q: A horizontal or nearly horizontal system acting to transmit lateral forces to the vertical resisting elements, it includes horizontal bracing system.
questions.n: The diaphragm acts as a large horizontal beam that distributes lateral loads (wind/seismic) to walls or frames.

questions.q: The total designed lateral force or shear at the base of a structure.
questions.n: The total lateral force used for design, denoted as V, is the summation of all story forces.

questions.q: An element at edge of opening or at perimeters of shear walls or diaphragm.
questions.n: Boundary elements provide localized reinforcement at edges to resist concentrated stresses from lateral loads.

questions.q: An essentially vertical truss system of the concentric or eccentric type which is provided to resist lateral forces.
questions.n: Braced frames use diagonal members to form a vertical truss that resists lateral movement.

questions.q: An essentially complete space frame which provides supports for gravity loads.
questions.n: This system relies on a frame for vertical loads, with separate elements (walls/braces) for lateral loads.

questions.q: A combination of a Special or Intermediate Moment Resisting Space Frame and Shear Walls or Braced Frames.
questions.n: A dual system utilizes both a frame and walls/braces to provide redundant lateral load resistance.

questions.q: The form of braced frame where at least one end of each brace intersects a beam at a point away from the column girder joint.
questions.n: Eccentric frames deliberately offset the brace to create a 'link' that absorbs energy through shear or bending.

questions.q: The entire assemblage at the intersection of the members.
questions.n: The joint is the physical zone where different members like beams and columns meet and overlap.

questions.q: The horizontal skeletal member in a frame system, a beam.
questions.n: A girder is a primary horizontal member that supports smaller beams or concentrated loads.

questions.q: An element of a diaphragm parallel to the applied load which collects and transfers diaphragm shear to vertical resisting elements or distributes loads within the diaphragm. Such members may take axial tension or compression.
questions.n: Struts act parallel to the force to 'drag' or push the shear load into the vertical elements.

questions.q: The boundary element of a diaphragm or a shear wall which is assumed to take axial stresses analogous to the flanges of a beam.
questions.n: Chords act as the tension/compression edges of the diaphragm, similar to the flanges of an I-beam.

questions.q: Those structures which are necessary for emergency post-earthquake operations.
questions.n: Hospitals, fire stations, and emergency shelters are classified as essential and require higher design forces.

questions.q: That part of the structural system assigned to resist lateral forces.
questions.n: This is the formal name for the combined elements (frames, walls, etc.) that handle wind and seismic loads.

questions.q: The displacement of one level relative to the level above or below.
questions.n: Drift specifically refers to the horizontal displacement between two adjacent floors.

questions.q: The usable capacity of a structure or its members to resist loads within the deformation limits prescribed in this document.
questions.n: Strength is the technical term for the capacity of a member to carry a load without failing.

questions.q: The lower rigid portion of a structure having a vertical combination of structural system.
questions.n: The code defines the rigid lower part of a combined system structure as the platform.

questions.q: Horizontal truss system that serves the same function as a diaphragm.
questions.n: In buildings without concrete floors, steel bracing in the horizontal plane acts like a diaphragm.

questions.q: An assemblage of framing members designed to support gravity loads and resist lateral forces.
questions.n: A structure is the technical name for any designed system of connected members that resists loads.

questions.q: A structural system without complete vertical load carrying space frame. This system provide support for gravity loads. Resistance to lateral load is provided by shear walls or braced frames.
questions.n: In this system, walls perform both gravity and lateral functions without an internal frame skeleton.

questions.q: A structural system with essentially complete space frame providing support for gravity loads. Resistance to lateral load is provided by shear walls or braced frames. High-Yield Strength Quenched and Tempered Alloy Steel Plate, Suitable for Welding.
questions.n: This is the correct designation for the specific type of high-yield steel plate mentioned.

questions.q: True or False, Bar larger than 32mm in diameter shall not be bundled in beams.
questions.n: The code limits bundling of very large bars in flexural members like beams due to bond and spacing concerns.

questions.q: Minimum concrete cover for a Prestressed concrete for beams and columns for primary reinforcements.
questions.n: The code specifies 40mm as the standard protection layer for primary prestressed reinforcement in these members.

questions.q: In a material under tension or compression, the absolute value of the ratio of transverse strain to the corresponding longitudinal strain.
questions.n:
This ratio (denoted by 
𝜈
ν) describes how a material narrows when stretched or widens when compressed.

questions.q: In column, the ratio of its effective length to its least radius of gyration.
questions.n: This ratio determines the buckling potential of a column; higher values mean the column is 'slender'.

questions.q: A quantity which measures the resistance of the mass to being revolved about a line.
questions.n: Torsion is the technical term for the twisting of a member about its longitudinal axis.

questions.q: A type of concrete floor which has no beam.
questions.n: A flat slab transfers loads directly to columns (often with drop panels) without using intermediate beams.

questions.q: The tendency for one part of a beam to move vertically with respect to an adjacent part.
questions.n: Shear is the action of parallel internal forces that try to slide one section of a member past another.

questions.q: A change in shape of a material when subjected to the action of force.
questions.n: Deformation is the general term for any change in size or shape of a body due to applied forces.

questions.q: The maximum value of tension, compression, or shear respectively the material sustain without failure.
questions.n: This is the stress level at which a material begins to deform plastically and is often used as the failure benchmark in design.

questions.q: It means that by which a body develops internal resistance to 'stress'.
questions.n: Stress is physically defined as the internal resistance of a body to an external force.

questions.q: The greatest stress which a material is capable of developing without permanent deformation remaining upon the complete release of stress.
questions.n: Allowable stress is the safe limit set by codes to ensure the material stays within its elastic range.

questions.q: Intensity of force per unit area.
questions.n:
Mathematically, stress is defined as Force (
𝑃
P) divided by Area (
𝐴
A).

questions.q: Loop of reinforcing bar or wire enclosing longitudinal reinforcement.
questions.n: Ties (for columns) and stirrups (for beams) hold longitudinal bars in place and resist shear.

questions.q: The measure of stiffness of a material.
questions.n: Stiffness ratio compares the stiffness of different members, acting as a general measure of rigidity.

questions.q: The failure in a base when a heavily loaded column strikes a hole through it.
questions.n: Punching shear is a localized failure where a column or pile 'punches' through a slab or footing.

questions.q: The deformation of a structural member as a result of loads acting on it.
questions.n: Deflection is the vertical or horizontal displacement of a member due to bending or axial loads.

questions.q: Nominal thickness of of a timber.
questions.n: Timbers are generally defined as having a minimum nominal dimension of at least 5 to 6 inches.

questions.q: The sum of forces in the orthogonal directions and the sum of all moments about any points are zero.
questions.n: Equilibrium exists when all forces and moments acting on a body are balanced, resulting in no net acceleration.

questions.q: The complete records of tests conducted (slump, compression test, etc.) shall be preserved and made available for inspection during the progress of construction and after completion of the project for a period of not less than.
questions.n: Building codes require these vital quality control documents to be kept for at least two years post-completion.
